I am 72 yrs old and I do not get too excited about games that much but this one was special. I found this game fascinating. Different style of play than FO3 or FO4, which up until now I used as a standard for playing games. I did not care for Metro 2033 so I did not pay much attn to these games. A friend said try it so I did and boy am I happy about that. Talk about a game you can put yourself into and become fully immersed, this is it and the artwork and graphics were incredible. Some things I did not care for but the good so far outweighs the bad it is not worth mentioning the bad. VERY NICELY DONE. I am keeping this installed and will play it again when I finish some others. (EDIT) I stated I did not care much for Metro 2033, I was wrong. I am playing the redux now and love it. Someone said to read the books, as soon as I am finished playing 2033, Last Light and Exodus in the proper order this time, I am going to do just that.

I just completed the series in the proper order, playing Exodus for the second time. I found it this time around even more magnificent than I did the first. I have experienced MANY thing in my many years so there is not a lot that will get to me. No game I have ever played affected my very inner being as this one has. I know of nothing else I can say without sounding like I am rambling so my last words will be WOW, absolutely f***ing WOW!!!!!

As i grow older, i tend to lose motivation to play games since alot of them aren't even fun anymore and i usually have to force myself to play them. But THIS game is an absolute must play, i absolutely loved every second of it. Some people may be scared off because of the change from linear gameplay to a more open-world type gameplay unlike it's predecessors. But i think they executed this change of pace perfectly.

The gameplay is basically the same as the previous games, they added a cool crafting system (that somehow magically turns some random chemicals and metal into gas mask filters and ammo). Your guns can get jammed if you don't clean them often and you have to manually unjam them, sand, snow, and even falling in water affects how fast your gun gets dirty. Your gas mask can get damaged too, and if it cracks you can repair it with duck tape (it's only temporary though), and unlike the previous games you can't pick up a new mask, you will have to repair this one at a workbench.

The morality system makes a comeback, but there's not alot of moral points to be earned in each chapter, most of it is straight forward unlike the previous games (also as a tip, listening to dialogues won't give you morality points, but it can give you sidequests and cool marks on the map).

The locations are really cool, there's a chapter for each season of the year, and you get to experience quite some interesting landscapes, ranging from snowy landscapes to desert places. I'd say the first chapter (The Volga) is probably the Highlight of the game, but that does NOT mean the other chapters are boring.

I haven't encountered any major bugs, most of the bugs i've encountered were physic bugs, and those were extremely rare, there are some game breaking softlock bugs supposedly, so make sure to back up your saves as you progress (i made a special folder where i kept all my saves from the beginning of the game to the end)

The best aspect of the game for me is probably how immersive it is, i haven't been immersed in a game like this in a really long time, in my opinion, i'd say it even takes the spotlight away from the first game.
And it's not only the "horror" elements of immersion, it's the family and friends aspect as well, drinking and playing the guitar with your friends on the train was one of the most real scenes i've ever seen in a video game, and i am so glad that a video game could capture that beautiful feeling.

Okay i'm getting quite stupidly philosophical there, to wrap it up, this game is AMAZING. It absolutely blew my mind, i thought it would kinda disappoint me after the first two amazing games, but it's quite the contrary. I think this is my favourite metro game, and i absolutely recommend it even at full price.

P.S. I highly recommend playing this game on the Ranger Hardcore difficulty as with all the metro games, not only does it help you immerse better, but i think it's the best way to experience this masterpiece of a game.

R.I.P. Андрей Корзинкин

This is one of the few series of games I have ever played where the next installment is better than the last. Normally, this is not the case, but Metro is a no ordinary game. The story really makes you feel a part of Artyom's family. Over the course of the series you bond with Artyom's mates in a way that feels closer than family. You care about everyone's well being and you want to play through the story to make sure everyone remains safe. Not only that, but the development of each and every individual character is wonderful. There's a lot of depth to them and you hear it in random conversations when you stumble upon them or smoke with them on the train ride. Hearing every word that everyone has to say any time really does mean a lot. 

The Soundtrack. I can not justify verbally how incredible the soundtrack is for this game. The emotion, the feeling, the atmosphere, the intensity is something that sounds like it was composed by a supernatural deity who knew music better than any human composer. The soundtrack perfectly harmonizes with the atmosphere of the game and setting that you find yourself in.

I honestly cannot get enough of this series. I played with Xbox Game pass on PC (88 hours) and waited to buy it on steam to show my fellow Ukrainian Developer my support!

One of the few 10/10 games I would say that is more than deserving of that rating.

In the game, we return to a post-apocalyptic future in which human civilization has been destroyed by a global nuclear war, and we once again assume the role of Artyom, known from the previous installments. The heroes travel across Russia aboard the Aurora train, searching for a place free from radiation and mutants where they can start a new life.


✅The game includes two DLCs, which I highly recommend playing. I liked the two different storylines.
✅The game has two endings: good and bad, and you can play through the game in two ways: loud or silent. This has a powerful ending at the end.
✅The game is well-optimized.
✅You have to be careful who you kill, because it also affects who you shouldn't kill at the end of the game.
✅The game features a more open world than previous installments.
✅Fantastic atmosphere, whether in the underground, the wasteland, or the forest.
✅The graphics look amazing, especially the lighting, which deserves a big plus.
✅Excellent dialogue and characters.
✅Variety of weapons, which we can craft ourselves, increasingly better weapons in the later stages of the game, and find various other weapon upgrades on the map.
✅You can find various collectibles and Artyom's journal entries, which provide a lot of information about the world and characters, and most importantly, how the main character views it.
✅We can also craft first aid kits, arrows for weapons, and grenades, but we need the right materials for this.
✅Interesting and gripping plot that keeps us in suspense until the very last hours of play. The story of Artyom, who sets off on a dangerous journey beyond the metro in search of a new life, is full of twists and turns and emotions. The characters are deeply developed, and their fates evoke sympathy and interest in the player. 
✅Various enemies
✅Locations are well-designed for stealth
✅The price is really good for such an excellent game
✅The sound in this game is amazing

❌Too few side missions.
❌A lot of running around, and not every location has the option to drive, which is a slight downside for me.
❌The downside to this game (and the previous installments) is that the main character unfortunately doesn't speak, but I still had a great time
❌The AI system was sometimes weak; enemies simply couldn't see us at close range, and mutants also behaved strangely.

I must say that I will cherish this experience for a long time to come and give credit to the developers for a wonderful job.

[h1]Overview[/h1]
[b]Metro Exodus[/b] is the third installment of the acclaimed series, inspired to the books of Dmitry Glukhovsky, and set after the events of Metro last Light. Once again impersonating Artyom, players will soon leave the cryptic tunnels of the Moscow Metro to journey on through the entirety of Russia, ending up in a variety of places ranging from deserts to lush forests - accompanied by Colonel Miller and his elite Spartan team. What initially begins as a daring escape soon turns out to be a journey for survival, as unexpected turns of events one after another come crashing down on the squad.

🟩 [b]Pros[/b]
[list]
[*]Incredible visuals with excellent art direction.
[*]Realistic, satisfying and unforgiving combat system on higher difficulties.
[*]Meaningful exploration with many secondary locations.
[*]Excellent narrative and character building.
[*]Overall good variety of content, situations, enemies and tools. 
[/list]
🟥 [b]Cons[/b]
[list]
[*]Karma system, which determines the ending, was reworked in a bad way.
[*]In Ranger Hardcore mode, Autosave frequency is inconsistent and can lead to significant progress loss.
[/list]
[h3]Rating: Excellent[/h3]
[url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1989090445]Click here for the complete Rating Chart[/url]

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2138850199

Starting with the good points, the strongest feature of Exodus as it was with the prequels, is the atmosphere and world-building, which deliver an uncompromisingly realistic take on the nuclear post-apocalypse. This time it's not confined to the cramped Metro tunnels, but shows in full the entirety of Russia's wastelands, and does so flawlessly. Fighting any kind of enemy on the higher difficulties is a tense and unforgiving affair, where all but the weakest attacks mean certain death for both yourself and most enemies. 

This realism is complemented by accurate gunplay and good variety of murder tools to use. Exploring the wastelands is not only spectacular but also worthwhile, as every map contains a bounty of secondary locations often hiding unique upgrades for Artyom's suit and weapon mods. They will make your life easier once acquired. The narrative and characters stay true to the excellent book series and do not disappoint in the slightest.

There are however a few dents to an otherwise flawless execution. The Karma system has been reworked and forces players to take on the majority of situations with complete stealth, without also killing anyone in order to get the good ending. This goes as far as penalizing you for killing someone that shot first and is openly hostile, while the consequences will influence your companions' very lives as if some "higher power" was there to punish you - which makes no sense. 

[b]Overall, Metro Exodus remains an excellent open-world FPS that delivers the quality already made famous from the previous chapters, at the same time enhances the gameplay in new ways bringing it to a new level that surpasses the previous ones in almost every department. It took me around 25 hours to finish the game on Ranger Hardcore, while exploring thoroughly every map and completing all side content. For the price of 40€ and excellent quality, I can recommend buying at full price.[/b]

[h1]In-Depth Breakdown[/h1]
🎮 [b]Gameplay Analysis[/b]
Gameplay is divided into Exploration, Character Management, Quests and Combat.

[b]Exploration[/b]
Is performed on foot most of the time, except in a particular map where there will be a truck at your disposal. Ziplines and boats are also used sparingly to traverse otherwise impossible paths. While exploring, keeping an eye out for mechanical and chemical components - both used in crafting - is one of the primary goals, as you'll need them to craft supplies. Of course you can also find already made ammo, medkits and filters, but that's a more rare occurrence. 

Certain specific places hold unique modifications more or less hidden, and this is what makes exploring every corner worthwhile. A global map will display your position and all the discovered points of interest, highlighted on the map by using the Binoculars on a high place. Safehouses are sparingly set around the world and they can offer a safe refuge to wait night or day, craft at the workbench and more importantly save the game if you play Hardcore. There is no fast travel.

[b]Character Management[/b]
Can be done on the fly with the portable workshop in your backpack, or in a more complete manner at a stationary workbench in a Safehouse. You will be able to modify any of your weapons with previously acquired mods at any time, as well craft simple ammo types such as arrows or steel balls, medkits and filters. More complex crafting requires a full bench and that includes changing your suit upgrades, crafting bullets and as well throwables like grenades, cleaning weapons to prevent malfunction.

[b]Quests[/b]
Are not numerous in the game and usually are about retrieving a specific item for one of your travel companions or another character. They do not always award anything other than achievements or Karma, but still they are worth doing for the sake of storyline and to explore new places.

[b]Combat[/b]
Is one of the most consistent elements of the experience and at least on the higher difficulties, is a brutal and unforgiving affair where even just one shot can instantly kill you, as well as enemies. Ammunition is fairly limited, while grenades and throwables are powerful bit very expensive to create - using all your resources, stealth as well, is key to prevail against overwhelming numbers. Nothing prevents you from going in guns blazing but on higher difficulties it's a good idea to take out at least some enemies silently before doing so. 

Foes range from your average bandit with a shotgun to nine feet tall abominations with the strength of twenty men, passing from mutated shrimps and venomous giant worms. Each foe has strengths and weaknesses for you to exploit, for example most animals will be scared by fire or your vehicle. Human enemies are definitely smart and use tactics such as flaking, cover and grenades to overpower you, other than having swift reflexes and excellent aim - on Hardcore at least. Being accurate, fast and conservative are the pillars of Metro's combat.

[b]Technical[/b]
[u]PC Specs: RTX2080Ti, Ryzen 3900X, 32GB RAM DDR4[/u]
[b]Critical Problems:[/b] None.
[b]Optimization:[/b] Resource usage is within expected parameters for the quality, no problems to report.
[b]Performance:[/b] The game runs without issues in 1440p, 85Hz on Ultra settings. 
[b]Bugs:[/b] Key rebinds do not work properly for certain keyboard configurations.
[b]Other issues:[/b] Save system on Hardcore difficulty has frequency issues, might be a bug, unconfirmed.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
Metro Exodus is definitely a worthy successor that expands the prequels' gameplay, taking it to new heights, but not without some drawbacks. Fans of the series and those who like atmospheric games will not be disappointed.

[h1]Positive Aspects[/h1]
🔹Amazing Visuals with a Photo Mode.
🔹Great Story.
🔹New Crafting system.
🔹Staying traditional. ( Metro 2033 & Last Light ).


[h1]Negative Aspects[/h1]
🔸Performance.
🔸Epic Store.


[h1]Introduction[/h1]
Metro Exodus is the third game after Metro 2033 and Metro Last Light and is the first one that offers Open World yet will stay traditional to the previous Metro games we all loved.

[h1]Review[/h1]
[list]
[*][h1]Gameplay:[/h1]

[b]Basic Mechanics & Tradition of Metro:[/b]
Just like in every Metro game, surviving is key. You should not waste Ammo and basically you have to be very efficient with it because when running out of ammo you're extremely vulnerable to enemies.Keep your flashlight recharged as it is a must have in the Metro trilogy. Stealth was always a decent part of the previous parts, does it still exist in Metro Exodus? Yes you can always use the shadows to your advantage, NPCs even mention it when you have to raid a checkpoint with thieves that you should do so when its night time as some of them are sleeping and others cannot see you in the darkness. What I liked it is that the people kept some key mechanics like recharging, gas masks,medic needles and the Map and objective board the thing is that these mechanics do not really play a huge role anymore now that Metro Exodus play out in a less contaminated area yet they kept it traditional and kept all the mechanics and even improved them a little as the gas mask can get damaged which gives you the change to seal the hole. A nice addition was that you can upgrade your armory, a much more advanced compass that can give you multiple information like how many enemies you have and from where they are coming etc. , the Geiger Counter ( device that counts ionizing radiation (r/hr)) got improved as well as it is much easier to understand how toxic the area you're in is. Simply said that Metro Exodus stayed a Metro game to the core.

[b]Weapons and attachments:[/b]
Just like in every Metro you can choose between multiple types of weapons like AR, SMG, DMR, SR, LMG, Shotguns, Pistols, revolvers and pneumatic ones that do not require expensive materials to create ammo. Simply said this is the classic Metro loadout and you choose 3 weapons and you can easily customize them on a workbench that is scattered around the Open World maps, you can put different optics, grips, magazines, FOOKING LASER SIGHTS ( rainbow six siege reference ), and other things. They even added something that I haven't seen since Far Cry 2 and that is that weapons become worse with time which makes you clean them so they do not jam, great additions!

[b]Open World:[/b] 
Lastly I will tackle the Open World and it basically looks like Mad Max & Metro and Fallout had a baby and it honestly was great in my opinion. After every major ''Act'' you change locations and it makes the game a lot more enjoyable to see different locations that I could never think of in the previous Metro titles there obviously isn't much to do except some side mission that are been given next to the Main ones but this is the Wasteland don't forget this, it has been a pleasant surprise that they made a nice yet traditional to the Metro series open world.

[*][h1]Story:[/h1]
[h1]Spoilers Ahead![/h1]
Metro Exodus has been a roller-coaster of surprises for me, first you find yourself in Moscow on top of a building looking for Radio activity because you're sure that there are more people alive, after fighting your way back to the Metro after being attacked by mutants and getting radiated Anna and Coronel Miller demand that you should never do it again, as always Artyom decides to take Anna and do it again and surprisingly enough you discover that people still exists, after some time you're getting captured by some other Russians and Artyom is apparently getting shot in the chest but saved from a military tag ( how original ). Well after all that Artyom finds a base and decides to investigate and save Anna, in all that craziness they find out that this is an official military Russian base that has built jammers all around Russia in order to hide themselves from the other countries as the world war was still going on, after all of that they are been looked at as Spies and the whole team decides to find a quite place with clean air etc. After lots of adventures Anna gets sick and you and Miller decide to go to the most polluted are in Russia to get her her medicine, that is where the classic Metro two way story come to life. In the bad ending both you and Miller die and drive the train to eternity etc and overall it gives you a very depressive feeling in the other ending only you survive because Miller used his stempak in order to save you and that made him die sadly but you find the place you where always looking for and can live on in peace etc. Great story in my opinion.

[*][h1]Graphics/ Audio:[/h1]

-Visuals:
Metro is easily one of the best looking games and you really don't need someone to explain to you that it looks good.
Characters really look real life like and you can instantly understand their mood and emotions, lighting and textures are simply top notch and the overall design of the map and surroundings are perfects!

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1692642606

-Audio/Soundtrack:
Voice acting is great in the English language but I would 100% suggest everyone to play it with the Russian voice actors as it feels that much much better and it actually helps the experience. Soundtrack is a Metro classic which captures the Metro series to the fullest. Great work as always!

[*][h1]Performance :[/h1]
-On Low End Devices:
Doesn't run at all.
-On Mid End Devices:
AMD FX-8370E,16GB RAM, Nvidia GTX 1060:
Runs ( comment section).
-On High End Devices:
Intel Core i7 4790k, 16GB, Nvidia GTX 1070:
I was able to run the game on Maxed out settings with +60fps in 1080p.

-Bugs/Glitches/Crashes:
I had no Bugs but I had some glitches not per say gamebreaking but corpses that got killed in a gun fight got stuck between some objects which made me not be able to collect their items, lastly I had no crashes in around 21 hours of great Metro gameplay. Keep in mind I had some FPS drops in random moments but other than that the game worked surprisingly fine for me.

[*][h1]Price :[/h1]
Well, they made a deal with Epic so yeah...that is a bit awkward. Still I would pay the 60 Eur. because Metro Exodus simply has more content than the previous titles yet has identical or even the same quality to it.
 
[*][h1]Conclusion :[/h1]
Metro Exodus was a risky Open World project for the Metro series yet it surprised me a lot that they kept the game very traditional to the series and made some key additions in order to make it feel like something new still, easily in my GOTY running.

[h1]Overall Rating:  90/100[/h1]

Recommended if you want to clean your dirty post WW2 Russian Kalashnikov !

Let's get this out of the way: Removing the game from Steam two weeks before launch and making it an Epic exclusive was a stupid, greedy and anti-consumer decision. Shame on you Deep Silver for doing that. Many people will not be able to enjoy this fantastic game because of you. Now, on to the review.

I love the Metro series. Metro 2033 is one of my favorite games ever. Despite its overall roughness, it has an atmosphere unlike any other game, and a fantastic story. Last Light is in many ways a better game than 2033. It has improved gunplay and stealth, and is a much more polished game. I wasn't a fan of the story and the characters (Khan is a completely different character, Anna is handled very poorly), but it is still a great game. I've played both of these games and their Redux versions multiple times, so I guess you can say I was looking forward to Exodus, and I'm happy to say, I'm not disappointed.

Story takes place one year after Last Light and it is a sequel to the last book, Metro 2035. For reasons I won't spoil, Artyom and his wife, Anna, together with some friends, go on a journey across post-apocalyptic Russia on a train. Despite some problems, the story is overall good, but I think the real highlight of the game is the characters. I genuinely cared for all of them, I laughed and cried with them, and I did everything I can to make sure all of them made it alive to the end. There is an insane amount of optional dialogue you can listen to that helps you understand the motivations of the characters, and I applaud 4A Games for their effort.

During this journey you come across mini open world levels themed after different seasons. I say 'mini open world', but that's not a bad thing. Despite spending a lot of time on the surface, it is still a linear game, but you are given the option to explore if you want. Rest assured, you won't find mindless side missions or collectibles in this game like you would in a Ubisoft game. It is still Metro. Especially that final mission. It's one of my favorite missions in the entire Metro franchise. Level design is great and the game looks gorgeous, which makes the exploration that much more fun. Not to mention, you'll find new weapon parts, ammo and crafting materials by exploring, so it is definitely encouraged. Speaking of crafting materials, let's talk about the crafting system. This game doesn't have the trade system from the previous games, instead you craft your own equipment by finding materials. You can craft medkits, filters for your gasmask, or even ammo. You also need to regularly clean your weapons, because if they get too dirty they can jam, and trust me you don't want that during combat. To clean your weapons, you need to find a workbench, but most of the crafting and weapon customization can be done on the fly. Customizing your weapons is so much fun. Just came out of a bandit camp but now you have to deal with far away mutants? You can turn your silenced revolver into a sniper rifle by slapping a long barrel, a sniper stock and a 4x scope on that bad boy. 

Now, let's talk about some problems. For me, the biggest problem in Metro Exodus is how clunky the movement feels. You get stuck on everyting, and climbing objects is very frustrating. Sometimes the object you are trying to climb pushes you back, and you need to repeatedly try the same climb until it finally plays the climbing animation. Another one is the hit detection on your guns. Sometimes, your bullets don't connect to enemies, like a Treyarch game. You can aim perfectly, with a fully clean gun, and the bullet will go to a random direction. This may sound like a small problem, but it can cause you to get detected during a stealth section, so it is a big problem. I once lost 10 minutes of progress on a stealth section, because my gun fired to a random object instead of the enemy in front of me, and he turned and one-shotted me on Ranger difficulty.

Another big problem is the voice acting. Metro games always had bad voice acting but Exodus easily has the worst. What's even worse is, characters talk over each other. For example A and B are speaking. A is asking B a question, but B starts answering the question before A has finished asking it, so there are a few seconds in which they talk at the same time, and this happens more often then you think. Turning on the subtitles helps a little, but it is still annoying. Also, the game has many bugs and glitches, ranging from funny graphical errors to your save file getting deleted. Thankfully, 4A has patched a lot of these, but they definitely have more work to do. The final big problem is the options menu, or the lack of one. You have almost no options to customise. Can't turn off anti-aliasing or shadows, also DX12 causes many people's games to crash. There is no FOV slider, instead you have to config files to change it. Come on guys, it's 2019, please put a little more effort on your options menu.

Metro Exodus is not a flawless game, but then again, no game is. I played this game for 44 hours in 4 days. I literally took a break from life and played Metro Exodus. If you are a Metro fan, play Exodus. The open world aspect of the game doesn't take away from the atmosphere. If you haven't played a Metro game before, and want to start with Exodus, you can definitely do that, I don't think you'd be confused, also the characters are mostly new. Though you should play 2033 and Last Light, I mean come on! I'd say Exodus is better than Last Light but not as good as 2033, but all three of them are must-plays!

[h1]Metro Exodus.[/h1]
[i]Out of the Metro, into the Aurora.[/i]

[i]Note: I played this game offline, which is why my hours-on-record are so low.[/i]

[b][u]Introduction[/u][/b]
Metro Exodus is hands down the crowning achievement of the Metro franchise. It brings Artyom and company out of the claustrophobic metro tunnels of 2033 & Last Light, and into the daylight of POST-apocalyptic Russia, in all its glory. Never before has a game so effectively blended the polish of a linear FPS with the freedom of a reactive open world, while capturing a Slavic atmosphere which rivals that of blin-kingpin S.T.A.L.K.E.R. itself. Exodus takes Metro to fantastic new heights while cutting out nearly all the lows, whether that be in gameplay, world-building, or storytelling. As a fan of the series for years, I’m happy to report that this [i]is[/i] the sequel we were waiting for.

[b][u]Plot[/u][/b]
Metro Exodus begins with the protagonist, Artyom, plagued by the suspicion that there is still human life left on the surface beyond the Moscow Metro system. You, as Artyom, have been making frequent dangerous excursions to the surface since the end of the previous game in the hopes of finding a radio signal to validate this theory. This causes strife with your wife, Anna, who is fearful that one day you won’t arrive home still breathing. As a consequence, she decides to come with you on one of your trips to the surface to watch your back. On that fateful day, Artyom and Anna discover; not a radio signal, but actual people who claim to hail from outside the city… as well as an operational locomotive train, capable of taking them – and the Spartan Order – across the country.

[b][u]Presentation[/u][/b]
Shifting to the graphics of Exodus, I have to say that they are entirely up to series standards. The art style is identical to that of its redux-ed predecessors, but every visual detail has been tweaked to breathtaking fidelity. Textures are photorealistic, faces are way beyond the uncanny valley in a positive direction, animations are fluid and numerous, the lighting is gorgeous to the point that its beauty exceeds real life, and all other technical components are practically flawless. The soundscape is noticeably (mostly) unchanged from the previous games, however there is a whole new soundtrack which accompanies Exodus’s atmosphere terrifically. As for performance, the game is demanding, but still well optimized. All in all, I’m absolutely taken by Metro Exodus’s presentation.

[b][u]Exploration[/u][/b]
Exodus is divided into roughly three separate maps throughout the course of the game, as well as a few more linear levels. While the settings themselves are gorgeous to the eye, from the swamps of the Volga River to the deserts of the dried up Caspian Sea, there’s also a lot to do. Each region has multiple objectives and locations, with secrets to uncover and loot to seize. There is a disparate theme to the individual provinces too, giving Exodus a real sense of variety. Notes and audio journals dot the world-space as well, revealing the history of a place and its people following the war. The several environmental stories told are enlightening, and sometimes even heart-rending. Altogether, Exodus’s environments are impeccably designed, and reward intense investigation.

[b][u]Gameplay Mechanics[/u][/b]
Metro Exodus, among other secondary features, utilizes an all new crafting and modification system, which I’d say is… a mixed bag. The crafting component of the game feels lazy, as there are only two materials to work with: metals and chemicals, which (annoyingly) functionally constitute 90% of the games lootable items – meaning most valuable consumables must be crafted. On the modification side of things, there’s a lot more to like. There are roughly ten base guns in the game, but each can be radically altered to work more effectively in different scenarios. Gear modification serves as the progression system, so it’s important to stay up-to-date with your weapons and accessories. There are a few more gameplay mechanics such as stealth, radiation, and vehicles, but all can be roughly summarized as ‘well implemented.’

[b][u]Gunplay Mechanics[/u][/b]
The Metro series is known for its atmosphere, and the immersion of its combat is a central element. I truly believe Metro Exodus has perfected the first-person impact of firing a gun; between the recoil and sound design, and even on down to the stopping power of each individual weapon. And good news – from bandits to mutant beasts, and slavers to the eerie humanimals, there’s a whole host of new adversaries to blast away across the scarred face of Russia. The AI of human enemies is quite sophisticated too, being able to call out your position to their allies if they spot you; relative to the objects around you. It’s also worth noting that you can defeat humans non-lethally, and that combatants will surrender if routed. Intricacies like these nested within Exodus’ combat system are what drive the gameplay, and make it uniquely satisfying.

[b][u]Main Narrative[/u][/b]
Refocusing on Exodus’s story, it’s a much better tale than that of the previous titles. For reasons I won’t spoil; you, Anna, Colonel Miller, and the rest of the Spartan Order travel eastward through post-apocalyptic Russia in the train found at the beginning of the game, which is quickly coined the [i]Aurora[/i]. As the crew trek across the scorched earth of the motherland, seasons change, and new societies are discovered. The survivors of the nuclear holocaust have become vicious luddites, bandits, cannibals, and slavers – but a rare few have preserved their humanity. Eventually the Order’s goal becomes to find an untainted land to call home; a place where a civilized society can rebuild, and Artyom and Anna can raise a family.

[b][u]Characters[/u][/b]
Whereas in past Metro games the supporting characters were side-pieces or even something of a nuisance, Exodus is much more character-driven in its storytelling. The blank stares of Bourbon and Khan are gone; replaced by the sensitive compassion of Stepan, cockiness of the impressionable Duke, and the [i]believable[/i] love of Artyom’s wife, Anna. The Aurora’s crew grows and changes with time, developing through the experiences they endure and the trials they overcome. If you care to bend an ear, your comrades will talk it off, expressing their thoughts, plans, hopes, and fears. While the translation of dialogue to English can be clunky at times, the character writing itself is just magnificent. The inspiring humanity of this small group of characters truly bring your goals as Artyom into perspective. The people of Metro Exodus are what make the whole experience.

[b][u]Morality & Choice[/u][/b]
On a quick narrative note before my final verdict, I’d like to clearly express that Exodus tracks your moral status throughout the course of the 25-odd hour campaign. There are particular actions you can complete that will give you positive karma, and specific crimes you can commit that will accrue negative karma. How you interact with the game world and its characters will have consequences – not only in the form of separate endings, but in a cascade of different narrative outcomes. The Order’s exodus is a treacherous one, but the most perilous war is that of the one which rages [i]right through every human heart, and through all human hearts[/i].

[b][u]Conclusion[/u][/b]
I feel my opinion on this game has been made fairly obvious by this point, but that doesn’t mean I won’t praise it further. Metro Exodus is one of the best games, period, that I have ever played. Its the culmination of what already was a phenomenal series, and Exodus pulls no punches in giving the trilogy a stupendously vast, enjoyable, meticulous, touching, and downright impressive send-off. I couldn’t have imagined a better way to conclude Artyom’s journey.

[h1]Personal Rating: 10/10 – Practically Perfect[/h1]

Vibrant World, Beautiful Graphic, Satisfy Gunplay, Enjoyable Story, and Every action has consequence for the closure of the story. An overall fun experience.

Highly Recommend.

[h1]6 years[/h1] 

It took 6 years for [i]4A Games[/i] to develop and publish the 3rd (and perhaps final?) instalment in the Metro series. A long time but from the below you'll see that in my opinion it was worth it. As a little background to the journey I had with Metro: Initially, I didn't think much of the first game when it was released. I certainly found it interesting but I think [i]Last Light[/i] made the franchise really famous and these games playable. 

Stealth was improved, graphics and optimisation became better and releasing the 1st game in [i]Redux[/i] version was definitely an asset. One could clearly see a lot of work was put into it - it wasn't just needed for next-gen consoles like many of the remastered editions out there. Oh, by the way, I'm familiar with the first book, too, which is more like an adventure than action.

[h1]Going open world[/h1]

Frankly, I didn't expect this. After the prologue we find ourselves in a level called [i]Volga[/i] and we immediately notice the huge map we have at our disposal. Artyom is given clear instructions as to where to go but optional objectives will soon start popping up on the map. An interesting concept that increases the longevity of the game (and also encourages the speedrunners to step in and do a walkthrough as fast as possible).

The [i]Caspian[/i] level is the next major map that puts us into a completely new environment: instead of cold we experience heat for the first time in this desert. Humanimals are the new mutants that try to disguise themselves - after a while you'll be able to notice them and avoid any surprise attacks. In case you think the outdoors makes us forget the dark, foreboding tunnels of the metro you are wrong: we'll have several opportunities to go underground so prepare yourself for welcoming those nasty spiders once again. The desert level was the first where I really started using the game's built-in photo mode. 

[h1]Resource management & sleeping[/h1]

Two great things come from the sandbox approach: no more vendors i.e. ammunition as currency is not available anymore. I remember accidentally reloading my weapons with this ammo in previous instalments. Thank god the creators used a special effect for these bullets so I could quickly notice the mistake I did when shooting. With Artyom we now collect scrap metal and chemicals. We can craft ammunition and throwables - the excess we find is immediately scrapped down and get added to the quantity we have. 

We'll also need workbenches as some crafting can only be done there, plus, we have to repair our equipment and clean our weapons regularly. I really liked this new approach and as you can already guess things become more interesting under ranger difficulty. The weapon upgrades such as scopes or bigger magazines we scrap from enemy weapons.

Finding safehouses allows Artyom to sleep. Normally, day-night cycle is around 2 hours. Approaching an outpost with several watchguards is best done under nighttime as stealth is much easier this way. 

[h1]Brave New World[/h1]

Is what Artyom and the team are looking for in this game. In between missions we can spend some time on our locomotive. Have discussions with others so that we can get to know them better. Prepare for a lot of collectibles this time (not just 70 diary entries but more than a dozen postcards that are VERY hard to notice) and also don't forget the decisions you'll be able to make at key areas as once again we have two endings. There are no annoying requirements such as giving money to the poor or interacting with every single musical instrument - on my first walkthrough I managed to get the good ending by simply trying to help everyone (side objectives), sparing lives and choosing the stealth approach coupled with knocking out enemies instead of killing them.

[h1]Summary[/h1]

Exodus is a great sequel and continuation of Artyom's journey - now outside of Moscow. Graphics are superb, as usual, the game also has two story-oriented, no-nonsense (I'm looking at you, [i]Tower[/i] and [i]Developer[/i] packs) DLCs and also a [i]New Game Plus[/i] mode with lots of modifications we can choose from (24-hour day-night cycle. commentary mode, more radiation, fewer weapons etc.) the game refers to as mutations. Overall, a great package is what we have here and hats-off if you can manage to complete the game under ranger hardcore or in iron mode!

metro exodus is SO SO PEAK even tho i dropped it after 5 hours.

lemme explain.

i REALLY didn't like the first major chapter, the open world felt wrong for metro. no tunnels, no claustrophobia, no oppressive weight. the game starts out as metro, but turns into something far greater than og metro.

the world & story building in exodus is NEARLY unparalleled imo

from intense, claustrophobic action in the metro, to ridiculously detailed open world sections, exodus expands on the first 2 games in a way ive NEVER seen in a trilogy.

the story is LEAPS ahead of the first 2 games, by the end, i was genuinely stressed that it was going to end.

2033 had atmosphere, last light had personal stakes, exodus has both + an entirely new layer of story depth. artyom isnt just surviving anymore - hes actually trying to build something.

a life, a home, a family. the moral choices actually hit different when youve spent 50 hours with these people on a train.

the atmosphere is the best in the series. thats saying something. the tunnels of 2033 are iconic, the station politics of last light are sharp, but exodus shifts from dread to something more complex. the environments are genuinely insane; snowy forests, radioactive deserts, terrifying swamps, a dead city that raised my heartbeat more than OUTLAST did. each level has its own vibe, its own rules, its own rhythm. i loved every single one by the end, in a way that hasnt been replicated by any game ever.

combat is drastically improved, yet still lacking in some departments. its functional, but i must admit running over demons with a VAN was undeniably fun. the weapons feel weighty enough, the gun degradation system is a nice touch, but youre not here for the combat. you never were.

the open world fear is real but overblown, yes its entirely diff from the first games but its FAR from ubisoft bloat. every area has purpose, every side objective and character belongs.

It turns out that what makes Metro – a series named and known for its dark, subterranean survival-horror atmosphere – work was never really dependent on being underground at all. The third game, Metro Exodus, successfully brings its lengthy single-player campaign to the post-apocalyptic surface without sacrificing any of the series’ signature tension.

In an era where most first-person shooters seem to be intent on constantly upping the tempo, Metro Exodus is refreshing in its demand that you take your time. This is not a run-and-gun experience; it’s a stay-low-and-go-slow crawl through some of the most atmospheric and detail-rich settings I’ve ever experienced in a story-driven shooter. With a storyline that sidesteps the supernatural themes of its predecessors in favour of focussing on a more affecting human experience, and level design that affords you significantly more freedom without giving you too much room to relax, Metro Exodus feels like the full realization of this series’ potential.

[i] [b]Wow is all I can say. I have no words.[/b][/i] You know an ending is good when you think "No. No. That can't be it. There's no way." and then the reality hits you. That was it. And that was the ending you got. Wow. I have nothing but praise for this game, especially in the story aspects. [spoiler] I got the bad ending, and wow...Anna's speech at the funeral and the rifle volleys legitimately made me tear up. I did not at all expect that from this game when I started playing.[/spoiler]

I've seen the Metro series before on Steam, just browsing, but I dismissed it for whatever reason. At the time of writing this, I've only played Exodus, but if this one game is anything to go by, I wish I hadn't dismissed it so quickly. It's... I've gone speechless again. It's amazing. The chapters each have good and bad endings, another thing I didn't expect, and it made the game feel...surreal, the way it judges you, if that makes sense. The characters feel... like family. Like you have to protect them, even if it means putting your life and your beautiful,Russian-man body on the line. There's moral dilemmas that I didn't realize I made a bad decision on until it was way, way too late. ([spoiler] Shooting the bandits... I had no idea they were supposed to be young... It kinda made me feel bad. Them's some big ass kids though, damn dude!!![/spoiler]).

The gunplay is phenomenal. It feels... not realistic, that's impossible for a video game, in my opinion... It feels way more realistic than anything I've ever played, though. The way the guns are loud, a sharp crack in the silence, it's incredibly immersing. There are several guns, but I'll focus on the AK (Or Kalash/Kalashnikov, as it's called in this game). I haven't shot an AK, I've shot everything from pellet guns to AR's, but the way Artyom fires his AK is exactly what I expect it to be. A loud, sudden, sharp crack, followed by either a pained scream from the person or animal you just royally pissed off, or the deafening silence from whatever is on the recieving end of that barrel. Guns get dirty, and jam, too. It makes sense, to an extent, but it bothered me a little that Artyom could wipe blood or spider-goop off his visor easily in one swift *wipe*, but dusting that little bit of mud off the gun with his sleeve, his glove, or even a rag he may keep in his backpack? Heavens no, comrade. That's too nasty, even for big, strong, Vodka-loving Russian man.

Stealth matters too. It can change the ending of the game. I usually stealth through everything, until I get shot at, then I fire back. It's not boring stealth though. There's elements like light exposure, your position, enemy lines of sight, sound, all making it very engaging in practice. The enemy AI isn't completely retarded either. It can pass as realistic.

Easy 94/100. I cannot praise this game enough. There were only a few minor details, like the previously mentioned gun cleaning, that annoyed me in any way, shape, or form. I got it for $15.99 on sale on a whim because I was bored, and I found myself lying awake late last night, 7 hours into the story, thinking "I want to keep playing Exodus, but I need to go to bed already." [b] If nothing else in my review helps you decide if you buy this game or not, let it be that last sentence. I think that says a lot about the game.[/b]

Although I had some criticism towards the former two Metro games, in general I liked them. I was looking forward to play the third game, especially given that it was supposed to be very different from its predecessors. And that it was. Unfortunately, I can't say all changes were welcome.

First, what I liked about the previous Metro games is the atmosphere of the metro and remnants of humanity. There was a fine balance between spending time in the underground and on the surface, there were quality horror moments with a dose of mysticism. And for the most part, all of this is lost in Metro Exodus. Except for the last chapter (which, I think, is the best part of the game), most of the time you spend on the surface, underground bunkers are rare and optional and are not even close to replacing the metro. The suspense moments are simply nonexistent. The authors tried to set the mood by the post-apocalyptic scenery on the surface, but that is a poor replacement, especially given the gameplay. The game feels and plays as an open-world survival, with lots of resource hoarding and crafting. Looking at another crumbled shack or a rusted shipwreck you're thinking what kind of resources you might find there, not what kind of story is hidden in there. This simply kills that depressing atmosphere I was so fond of.

Second, the first two games had reasonably good stories. The first one was especially good, it even had a moral choice in the end. But I can't say there is much of a story in the third game. Basically, at the beginning of the game Artyom and a small crew of spartans leaves Moscow and travels around the country with no real goal. Sure, at certain points the game offers a reason to move forward, then, at the end of the chapter, it gives you a reason for the next one, and so on. But there isn't an ultimate goal or a feeling of progression towards it. Besides the simple kill/don't kill decisions, there aren't any moral choices in the game. What's worse even, there's no moral of the game, at all. In Metro: Last Light, there were kill/don't kill moments too, but you had a moral obligation to the Dark One, and the characters in M:LL were more complex and more familiar. All that made those decisions not so trivial. In Exodus, you barely even know the characters beside your crew, and there's barely any reason to make one choice or the other. Barring some details, the ending is more or less predictable, and, given how unattached you are to your companions, is mediocre. There are good and bad endings, depending on your choices during playthrough.

Speaking of the characters, they are one of the weakest parts of Metro Exodus. Some of the main companions are straight annoying in their sheer blind stupidity. ([spoiler]Yes, Miller, I mean you. How a whining tinhead like him managed to become a head of the spartans is beyond me. That man definitely does not have the wisdom and strength to lead the toughest stalkers of the metro.[/spoiler]) Every character in the game is 1D, shallow, straight as an arrow stereotype. You know them for 5 minutes, you know them to the end of the game. No shades of grey here, we are the good guys, most of them are bad. Aside from a couple of obvious main companions, the rest of the crowd are so unremarkable that you can barely tell them apart, if not by appearance. The dialogs, with the speechless Artyom and these dummies quickly become a farce, and you wish you could skip them. I have to say, stereotype characters were bad in the previous Metro games, especially M:LL, but even there they had some depth to them (remember Pavel?). In Exodus, it got much much worse.

What is good about this game is visuals and sounds. The game is beautiful, and in that regard it continues the Metro tradition. Although level design has bugs in quite a few places, like grass or objects hanging in the air or objects you can clip through. The game has dynamic day/night cycle, although at key points in the game time goes non-linearly, which can be apparent.

In conclusion, should you buy and play this game? If you're a fan of the Metro series, you don't need my answer - you will likely buy and play it regardless. And you might be slightly disappointed, like I am. Still, I think the game is worth playing once, especially if you like the more open-world direction the game is taking. Just don't get your hopes up and maybe wait for a sale on Steam. For the ones new to the Metro series, it is difficult to recommend starting your acquaintance with Exodus. I'd recommend playing Metro 2033 and Metro: Last Light first. Having played those first you'll have better understanding of the story and background of Metro and you can then decide if you want to play Exodus.

[h1] A Word on the Controversy	[/h1]

In light of all the upset currently surrounding Metro Exodus I wanted to provide my own, more middle of the road review. Everything I say here comes from someone who, while enjoying the Metro games, is by no means an overly supportive fan who would instantly love anything with the Metro name slapped on it. Nor am I willing to pretend I hate a game simply because others have decided it must be hated no matter what.

As it has been the subject of many debates already I am going to avoid beating a dead horse here and refrain from giving too much discussion over the decision to remove the game from Steam in favor of exclusivity on the Epic store. All I will say about this is that I find it to be a very underhanded move, but my frustration lies with Epic and Deep Silver’s corporate team, who are ultimately the ones who made this decision. I find the hate aimed towards the devs of Metro, who typically have no say in such decisions, to be misguided. Especially when they have obviously poured a lot of love into a game that has had its launch marred by a decision that was out of their control. 

I happened to preorder Exodus just about a week before the removal from Steam was announced, but in the interest of full disclosure I will admit that had I not happened to catch it at this time I would be waiting a year for it to be back on Steam so as not to support the Epic store.


[h1] The Good	[/h1]

[b] Setting & Gameplay	[/b]

First and foremost Exodus absolutely blew me away with the level design. You will find there to be a much greater variation in locations and scenery than ever before seen in a Metro game. Every single area you encounter is completely breathtaking in its own unique way, with an incredible amount of detail on just about everything. For a game that is meant to be played through slowly and deliberately this beautiful world-building absolutely pays off, as you find yourself really wanting to explore and take it all in. 

The world does manage to feel a lot more open than we might be used to with Metro, providing a lot more space for you to explore and figure out a stealthy approach into various situations. But this being said, the game is still very linear, as you are never wandering around aimlessly and still have various objectives which keep you moving straight from one area to the next. This feeling of having a bit more space and freedom provides a nice contrast to all of the time you will spend exploring dark, claustrophobia-inducing underground areas.

[b] Story and Characters	[/b]

I absolutely adore the characters, especially Anna, your ass-kicking wife. The game does such a good job at truly making you feel the love between her and Artyom, with their interactions coming off as being very honest and sincere. The story is very interesting and unique, and I found myself to be genuinely interested in seeing what would happen next. There are a number of lengthy cutscenes, which I found to be well-done and important to the story, but I feel it is worth mentioning as I know this is not for everyone. 

You will have chances to return to the train which is carrying you and your crew, a feature I greatly enjoyed. I really loved taking these opportunities to explore how the train had grown and changed, as well as interacting with the other passengers. This really helped give a feeling of realism to the characters, making you care about them and their fate.


[h1] The Bad	[/h1]

[b] Graphics Presets	[/b]

Overall I really enjoyed my time playing Metro Exodus, but there are a few glaring issues that need to be addressed. First and foremost, the optimization is absolutely terrible. Instead of being offered the ability to individually mess with each setting you are forced to pick from presets: Low, Medium, High, Ultra, and Extreme. This essentially forces you to pick whatever setting your rig can best handle, which means you will most likely be forced into a setting that is actually below the capability of your PC, simply because the next preset enables just one setting that is just slightly too much for your setup. Had there been more customization offered with graphics settings this could have been easily avoided.

[b] Bugs and (Not So) Invisible Walls	[/b]

Another issue I had with Exodus are the completely random obstacles and/or invisible walls that I would run into and get stuck on. On quite a few occasions when exploring (or even worse, during a fight) I’d find myself randomly unable to walk over an area that looked as if you should be able to walk through it. While I love and appreciate the huge amount of detail in this game, it’s very frustrating to lose a fight simply because you found yourself caught on a twig.

I also encountered a few bugs, mostly entertaining (like trying to leave my cabin on the train only to find myself soaring high above the map). But there were a few bugs that messed with my gameplay, most notably being an enemy that was somehow able to stick their gun through the wall to shoot at me. 


[h1] My Verdict	[/h1]

Exodus is a wonderful game that will greatly benefit from some patching. Had its release not been cast in a bad light due to a questionable business move then I feel it would be highly beloved right now. But those who are forced to wait until its return to Steam next year might actually find that this worked in their favor, as it will provide time for some final kinks to be worked out so that they may enjoy a great game the way it was meant to be played

GRAPHICS:
I got the game after playing (and loving) the first two in the series. I never saw any videos or trailers of it so I had no idea what to expect. I was completely blown away. The graphics in this game are stunning. Thus also requiring quite a machine to run it. I have the RTX 2060 super so i had no problem running it but my friend tried it with GTX 760 and had 30 fps on average on low settings.

STORY AND CHARACTERS:
Another strong point of the game is story. It is a character driven story and the game does a lot to make us connected to our companions. Between the missions I just stopped and listened to their conversations and banters and i just couldn't go on until they stopped. Each character has an interesting and distinct background and character, that surprisingly isn't bland and doesn't end up being a caricature. Relationships between the characters are amazing, and at certain moments one could get a teary eye.
In some places the plot falls a bit thin but then the characters relationships save them.

DIFFICULTY:
The game offers several difficulties to play with, which dictate the amount of ammo found in the world, how much damage you can take, how much health do enemies have... I played it on the normal difficulty and although it wasn't really hard, there were a few moments where i felt really vulnerable. But the real challenge comes with the Hardcore ranger, with it's rare ammunition, HUD turned off and constant sense of danger. 

GAMEPLAY:
The gameplay style is largely dictated by the difficulty and area. It goes from straight up shooter to almost horror stealth style. The gunplay is smooth, although i liked it a bit more in previous games of the series. The iconic weapon upgrades make a return, but i miss the unique currency in the shape of Military grade ammo. Stealth is really polished, but at some moments enemies randomly see you through a wall (happened to me only once or twice). I didn't really like the crafting but I guess it fits the open world style of those sandbox areas. At the end of the day it's still the original, slightly clunky Metro gameplay.

AUDIO:
Lastly I want to talk about the sound design. The soundtrack is phenomenal. It sets the mood for the game so nicely. It pumps intensity in certain moments and dread and sadness at others. It's one of the best soundtracks i heard in recent years. And the audio in general is really polished and high quality. Really a pleasure to ears.

tl;dr
I really enjoyed the game. The gameplay is enjoyable, be it shooting or stealth. The audio and graphics are phenomenal, but it needs a newer pc to fully enjoy the latter (although even on low and medium the game still looks amazing). The main game is about 25-30 hours long if you do some exploration, 15 more with dlcs. I think the game is well worth the price, but if you can get it on sale (i bought the gold edition for 25€) then it's a must buy.

Metro Exodus comes in two flavors: the base edition, and the 'enhanced' edition, which ray-traces every light source. It also provides DLSS, which downsamples the image, and then upsamples using ai to create an image that is indistinguishable from native resolution. In other words this game is simultaneously gorgeous and less demanding on hardware.

	I can't speak to how the base game looks minus ray-tracing, but the enhanced version looks amazing. Obviously this all depends on your hardware and how high you can push the settings, but with DLSS it's a visual treat for the majority. Being outside of the Metro allowed the devs to create lush environments with light sources other than dim candles and light bulbs.

	Anyone familiar with the franchise already knows what to expect. First person shooter with a bit more nuance to it than what is typical. You have a flashlight that needs manual recharging, weapons that cam jam and need cleaning, and a lot of little gadgets that you can customize. There's crafting of ammo, weapons, and upgrades now. Otherwise, same quality shooting as before. I miss the 'bullets as ammo' feature from the first game, but given that we're leaving the metro it wouldn't work anyway.

	The real selling point here is the 'open world' aspect of the game. The 'semi-open world'. Exodus features several maps. The introduction is as linear as ever. But once you're out in the world proper, you get what I'd call a 'mid-sized' open-world map. The story progresses linearly, but you also have side-objectives that present themselves. Not a lot, but enough of them. When it's time to pack up for a new location, we have a short intermission on the train before entering a new 'semi-open world'.

	I like it. It doesn't become GTA or Far Cry, so the narrative remains in-tact and you won't be spending days outside of the main plot. But it gives you more freedom of movement than the basic A to B map structure of most linear shooters. And it hammers home the 'survivalist' aspect of managing air filters and health because you can more realistically be in trouble away from base. 

	The only downside is that, narrative-wise we are leaving the Metro. We are searching for life outside of it. Which is fine, but we are also leaving a defining plot-point of the franchise: The Dark Ones. They're creatures that hide in the tunnels of the Russian Metro and have telekinetic abilities. The first two games established them as a misunderstood force for good that hold a connection with the protagonist. A connection that holds promise for rebuilding society in a post-nuclear war world.

	Because we are no longer in the metro, we no longer see them. Which is so...odd. THE plot point is just...dropped. The plot is logically moving to the next step, but it's abandoning half of the franchise lore and direction. It's very weird. Not bad, necessarily. Just...odd. 

	And while we're on it, I want to mention how long the characters yap on and on. About not much. You don't have to stick around for every character speech or interaction, but if you want the full story you'll feel obligated to. And wow do they babble on and on and on. I don't know if the intent was 'immersive' writing, but the effect was 'wow this guy won't stop talking get to the point'.

	I feel like the narrative is a missed opportunity, because it eliminates a lot of the mystique of the world. It goes in an interesting direction a quarter of the way through, before becoming a tale of finding somewhere to settle. Fair enough, but it's very 'basic' as opposed to the fantastical writing you'd expect of a game. There's a 'is the war still on-going?' subplot before being resolved, which is a bit of a shame. It feels like we left the dark ones and a lot of the interesting plot threads for the most sensible and realistic, but also the most basic.

I wanted to like this game. I really did. But there's so many problems with it in a multitude of areas.

I'll get to what I do like first. The audio design is excellent; The guns sound fantastic, the atmosphere is adequately eerie, and the occasional Kino song that pops up in the background is welcome (Go listen to Kino, they were a great band). The customisation for the guns also provides additional leeway for how one should tackle situations in regards to distance.

So what's wrong with it? Well let's get to the biggest issue for me; performance.

This game runs like SHIT. Utter fucking SHIT. No matter what settings I played on, I got this horrible micro stutter every few frames. I did eventually find a fix for it, which was to enable adaptive Vsync via NVidia Control Panel, but even then it still had a good chance of happening. It made the game unplayable for long periods of time. I did only have one crash though, so in that regard it did better than the previous Metro games, which used to crash a lot for me.

The second biggest problem is that the stealth is terrible and the game constantly berates you for not using it. Or better yet, it hounds you for killing people while stealthy. To top it off, the game heavily focuses on gun customisation, but apparently has no interest in you actually [i]using them[/i], at least not against humans. To make matters worse, there is only one way to non-lethally take out enemies, by knocking them out at close range. But with how bad the stealth is, doing that is a fool's errand.

The open areas are also extremely barren, and the best levels end up being the most linear ones at the start and end of the game. The psychological aspects of the game are also toned way down.

Overall, the game feels like it wanted to try new things, but didn't really execute all that well on them.
Like I said, I wanted to like this game, but I ended up being frustrated by the end of it.

Metro Exodus is a first person shooter set in the aftermath of a nuclear war, where a small group of survivors live in Moscow’s underground rail network. This is the third game in the franchise, following Metro 2033 and Metro Last Light. The player once again controls Artyom, as he leads a squad of soldiers on a quest across the country.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

• Combat is enjoyable and fairly challenging on normal difficulty.
• First 90 minutes feels very restrictive, with lots of lengthy dialogue scenes broken up by a few short combat sequences, during which you have an AI partner constantly saying “hey go over there, do this”. Thankfully, when you reach the open world sections, the game finally backs off and allows you to explore at your own pace.
• The world is a dangerous place, inhabited by several different types of enemies including Human bandits, Humanoid mutants, dogs, Watchmen (large wolf-like creatures that hunt in packs), flying demons, giant shrimp that live in lakes, giant spiders hiding in dark tunnels, and some boss level creatures that I won’t spoil. Occasionally you’ll notice the bandits and monsters attacking each other.
• Weapons feel great to fire, and include pistol, shotgun, assault rifle, sniper rifle, crossbow and the Tikhar, which uses air pressure to silently fire metal balls. Each weapon can be upgraded with mods to improve damage, accuracy, clip size, as well as changing how they function, such as different types of zoom sights or silencers. You can carry three weapons, which allows your loadout to have a nice mix of short range, long range and stealth.
• Its often a good idea to use stealth if possible, take out enemies silently, or avoid them completely to conserve ammo. Going loud usually attracts more enemies, and you can’t recover ammo from looting monster corpses, so you could quickly run out of ammo. You can craft more ammo, but crafting resources are limited and probably better spent on medkits and gas mask filters.
• Open world has a day/night cycle, and weather conditions like rain and sandstorms, which reduces visibility both for you and your enemies. Some areas are heavily irradiated, requiring you to wear a gas mask and change the filter periodically to avoid suffocating.
• Main story took 19 hours to finish. There are two different endings depending on your actions during the game. (I got the good ending :D)

[h1]Story[/h1]

• Main story is mostly well written.
• Voice acting is fine, but I’ve heard better. 
• Your squadmates don’t just exist to shoot stuff, they’re living their own lives.
• Artyom is a silent protagonist like Half-Life’s Gordon Freeman, which feels very weird because the other characters constantly talk to him during cutscenes. Its especially ridiculous every time they try to call him over a radio while on a mission. “Hey, Artyom, are you okay?”. Do they expect him to answer?

[h1]Technical[/h1]

• I suffered some frequent stuttering, even though my PC (i7 6700K @ 4ghz, 16GB ram, GTX 1080) is comfortably above the recommended spec shown on the store page. After adjusting some settings I had a constant 60 FPS, but occasionally it would freeze for half a second, which was very noticeable when turning my mouse sideways. Strangely, this was worse in the narrow underground tunnels at the start and end of the game, and it actually performed better in the open world areas. It never hurt me during combat, but it was annoying while exploring.
• Controls are fully rebindable, however there is a quite annoying bug. I prefer to use arrow keys for movement (yes, we still exist), but there are some scenes where you sit down while listening to an NPC talk and you have to use WASD to interact with objects, or to leave the conversation, meaning that I had to change my keybindings back and forth several times.
• When exiting back to main menu I frequently got a message suggesting that my saved games had been corrupted. I never actually lost any progress so I always just ignored the message, however you might want to research this further before purchasing. Maybe I just got lucky.

[h1]DLC[/h1]

• There are two DLC missions where the player controls different characters. The first takes place during the last mission of Artyom’s story, the second is set after the end of the main story.
• Combat is the same high quality as the main story. The first mission adds a flamethrower to the player’s arsenal.
• The stories are less detailed compared to the main story.
• The first mission is quite linear and lasts around 2 hours, while the second mission contains a new open world area and took me around 7 hours to finish.

[h1]Recommendation[/h1]

Metro Exodus has enjoyable combat and a good story, but is let down by some technical problems. As the game has already been out for a year on the Fortnite Kids’ Anti Consumer Store, I doubt these problems will be fixed now.

Still, its worth playing for fans of the FPS genre, and the Metro franchise. I bought the game plus DLC for 40% off, which feels like a fair price. If you’ve never played Metro before, I’d recommend picking up 2033 and Last Light, because they’re also really good.

A masterpiece of a game, I know this word is overused a lot, but truly one of the most immersive games Ive ever played, you don't play through metro exodus, you live through it. 

A wonderfully crafted story that will take you through different parts of russia, different climates, different times of year and weather, as you encounter all sorts of different crazy characters, lots of baddies but also some truly good ones, it feels like a journey of a lifetime and for most if not all the characters on board your train - it is. The game centers around your exodus from snowy nuclear winter moscow into the wilderness of the rest of russia, as you travel across it on a train fittingly named Aurora, the goddess of dawn. Each member of your crew feels like a real human being and they are all very talkative, happy to share with you their thoughts and feelings over a smoke break or a cup of questionable beverage, despite your character being mostly a mute (only ever talking during loading screens) the game plays with it pretty well. Sadly I can not tell you more about the story, because its a thing thats best enjoyed yourself without any spoilers or tips.

Now, why did I say it was immersive and you live through it, well simply put, its because it lets you become the main protagonist, it never breaks character and you feel as you are part of the story, you are not just a player, you are Artyom, there are no cutscenes, instead there are moments when you lose control of your character, but its all always done in first person, you shake hands, you hug characters, you give toys to children or items to your crew members, all done in first person. You get attacked by mutants and have to free yourself in first person with a quicktime event (which has several accesibility options so you dont have to mash a button like a crazy person), you row boats and drive vehicles, you push buttons and pull levers, open or close doors, but all with a proper animation, you have to recharge your flashlight manually with a portable charger, put your gas mask on and off, put the nightvision googles on, wipe the dirt off your mask, fix it up quickly, burn some spider webs with your lighter which can cause some spiders to crawl all over your hands and face and so much more that I am probably forgetting, but you get the idea. There is only really one menu of sorts and thats the crafting one, still the game tries its best to make even that feel realistic and part of the world too.

Now, all the immersion aside, what about the gameplay itself you might ask? Well its simply fun and allows for different style of play and approach, several different difficulty settings allow for any kind of player, from a casual to hardcore, from story enjoyer to immersion freak, you can set it all up yourself. You get to fight all sorts of different beasts but also humans. Speaking of humans, there are basicly always 2 options for you, stealth or combat and you always have the choice which one you pick. Combat is only forced in one single chapter/mission but i would argue you are not truly fighting humans at that point but rather beasts in human form, play it and see for yourself :) Stealth however is never forced on you. 

So you might be wondering, why would you ever want to stealth then? Well aside enjoying stealth itself you might wanna do it because of the karma system in this game, same as previous games, the ending of your game will depend on how much of a humanist you were during your playthrough. See, while there are factions in this game that are truly evil and they know it, those you are allowed to kill as much as you want, bandits, raiders, slave owners, you know, that kind, there are several factions that are not evil and are just defending themselves from you, the intruder into their world, with those, you might wanna rethink your approach and maybe try to stealth and spare them, speaking of sparing people, even the bad guys sometimes will surrender, as a rule of thumb the last survivor of a group of bandits prefers to surrender than die like the rest of his gang, at that point killing them would also give you bad karma. The karma system does not just end the game differently, it changes the way other characters react to your actions and interract with you, it changes the endings of several chapters of the game before the game end itself, all in all, as you might realise now, it calls for at least 2 playthroughs, oh and there is also new game +.

As far as DLC goes, both are great even if they play out fairly differently. The Two Colonels is a more linear one of the two, jumping between 2 different time periods and 2 different characters, hence the name, it tells a great story of the struggle of one colonel between his duty as a soldier and his obligations as a parent of a young child, a great story all in all, even if a sad one at that. Sam's Story is a bit more open one, like the base game, and takes place after the end of Metro Exodus main story, Sam, the only american in your russian crew takes on a long journey in his attempt to leave russia and finally come home to his parents that may or may not still be living in whats left of usa. Not only is Sam an interesting character in both the base game and the dlc (being an american in post nuclear war russia aint easy) but he is also voiced by the legendary Steve Blum, that you might know from Cowboy Bebop as the voice of Spike Spiegel. I forgot to mention, both him and the colonel from the other DLC are not mutes at all, since you are no longer Artyom, they talk and they talk a lot, both in-game and during loading screens, so prepare to hear lots from them during gameplay.

This review is getting kinda long, so ill try to wrap it up for you here. The graphics are great but also demanding, especially so the enchanced edition that you get for free for owning the base game, so do check the requirements and how well it performs online. The audio design is absolutely awesome, the music gives that extra atmosphere to the setting, be it during combat or calmer moments and overall the sound is solid, the weapons and monsters especially so, the guns feel powerful, loud and real and the mutants feel scary, strong and sometimes plain disgusting. (like giant spiders or worms, definently do NOT buy if you have arachnophobia). There are however occasional bugs,  I did not encounter anything game breaking, but I did see an occasional t-pose of an enemy i already killed or like when the combat music got stuck for me once and kept playing despite me being out of any combat and then just randomly fixed itself later, one enemy once phased through several tables and a window to get to me which gave me a light scare, the bugs are rare but they do exist, its nowhere near cyberpunk or fallout but its not 100% perfect either, so i felt i need to address it. Does it ruin the game? No, absolutely not and it gets my recommendation, It is a 10/10 game for me, that left me amazed and only wishing for more and a sequel. Speaking of sequels, Metro Exodus is a sequel, so I highly advice you get Metro 2033 and Metro Last Light, since its all one connected story, I would argue Exodus is a bit more independent from the previous games, still, you will not understand a lot of plotpoints if you have not played the previous ones and those games are masterpieces too, so get the whole trilogy when you get the chance. 

I came to play as Artyom for the third time, but instead I lived as him from start to finish, a wonderfully crafted story-driven adventure, that shows how do to both storytelling and immersion into the gameworld right, It grabs you and does not let you go till you are done, a rare but true 10/10, get it and you wont regret the money and time spent :)
