After the decision of the publishers to take the game away from Steam to make is Epic Store exclusive at the eleventh hour, I was put in a tricky position. Either I just turn my back to the game series or I purchase the game while I still able to do it on Steam. There is no need to discuss something that has been said a million times already regarding this situation. So this review is for the people who care about the game series and Metro universe in general instead of focusing on the Epic Store drama aspect.

My biggest fear was that Metro Exodus would lose its soul and atmosphere of the claustrophobic sense, in those narrow subway tunnels, full of bandits and creepy monsters, because of the developers’ decision to make a road trip game. Luckily, they were managed to keep the needed atmosphere despite the fact that all the events take place on a surface. However, I still have kind of mixed feelings about this game, simply because of the weird mixture of different locations and incessant feelings that Metro Exodus tries to refer to some other popular representatives of the genre. 

[h1] Story [/h1]

Metro Exodus starts with a short monologue of Artyom, briefly telling the players about what happened to him and his life during the events of the previous games. At the end of this monologue, he says he is not going to stop until he finds a way to stop this madness to come back to the normal life. During one of his regular raids, he finds a Soviet-era steam train called the Aurora. From that point, Artyom and a few Spartan soldiers begin a long journey across post-apocalyptic Russia to get the answers on the most important questions and find a good place to start a new life.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

Of course, the major innovation for the game series is that Artyom finally leaves Metro and goes on a big road trip alongside with his squad and beloved woman. During this road trip, they will make a series of different stops to complete certain objectives like finding a fuel, water or even a trolley to continue their journey. The diversity of landscapes and locations is absolutely amazing: first, you see an abandoned village full of crazy religious fanatics, then you end up in the desert with neverending sandstorms and in the next scene you are fighting against the wild forest people, etc. 

However, it’s really important to state that this game is not a classical open world game. Basically, it still remains the same linear game as it was before, the only difference is that the train makes stops from time to time and during these stops you have the ability to explore these lands. Don’t expect to see enormous maps with tons of different stuff to do: usually, it’s a pretty limited map with the main objective and a few side quests where you have to find some lost goods, get rid of the bandits or help someone who is in trouble. First I was excited and promised myself to finish all these side quests, but then I just got bored with them and focused on the main quest primarily, simply because they were not that special or interesting enough. 

You can clearly feel how Metro Exodus has been supported with a much bigger budget and it looks much more polished but still feels like the original Metro games. Now it’s simply stuffed with actions scenes with QTE and some breathtaking cutscenes during the most dramatic moments. At some point, there were too much of these scenes that I felt like I was already tired of those QTE and neverending madness on the screen. 

Following the traditions of previous games in the series, Artyom is always one step away from death. It happens so often that it just becomes funny at the end and the player starts to believe that this guy is simply immortal and extra lucky. I lost my account of how many times I was unarmed simply because someone attacked the protagonist again and he was able to survive or run away at the very last second. 

The game is much more improved in terms of the combat as well. At the very first moment when I got the chance to kill a monster from my AK-47, I felt a huge difference comparing to the previous games. Metro can be played in a stealth mode as well, where Artyom can turn off the lights, blow out the candles and shoot the lanterns to avoid getting caught. 

All these weapons can be modified and upgraded, this is something that has been improved as well. Now every single weapon slot has a preset, where you can choose which weapon you want to take for the next mission. Every single modifier that you find on the enemies’ dead bodies will be added to your inventory so you can attach them to your weapons next time you are near the workbench. 

The worst thing that Metro Exodus has from the previous games is bugs and glitches alongside with a not so clever AI. Sometimes enemies can just look in your direction and wait for a few seconds before start shooting and mutants can act really weird, especially at some absolutely dark levels. Not to mention texture stuck issues and some voice stuttering during the dialogues.        

[h1] Graphics [/h1]

Metro Exodus is absolutely gorgeous in terms of graphics. Through the whole journey, you will see the astonishing desert with the dried-out Caspian Sea, dull and atmospheric village full of crazy fanatics, beautiful sceneries of the frozen rivers and snowy mountains. I couldn’t stop admiring the detailing of each location and how they managed to work on them to bring us such quality content in the end. 

[h1] Sound [/h1]

Like every single game of the series, Metro Exodus is provided with a high-quality voice dubbing and atmospheric ambient sounds. It has some minor issues with stuttering and voices laying over each other from time to time, but it doesn’t happen that often to strongly focus on this.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

Metro Exodus is a massive project that has been developed with a soul and it tells you a great story about the journey, family and how it’s important to fight for yourself and for your happiness. The developers took a chance by creating a completely different game bringing the protagonists out of Metro on the surface and they didn’t fail. Highly recommended for every single Metro series fan.

[h1] Enjoy! [/h1]

For people who really enjoy the Metro series I would recommend the game when it’s on sale. The transition to open world suits metro very well. Most of the story and open world segments are great. However, the game is buggy and the core gameplay is completely broken on higher difficulties, which often makes the game more frustrating than fun, this is the only one I decided to not play on ranger. TL;DR: a bunch of mechanics have been added into the game that make it less fun than previous games. They also seem to have taken the annoying parts from previous games and made them even worse instead of fixing them. For a game that is built around player immersion there are a lot of mechanics in the game that make zero sense in the world and are very obviously there just to make the players life harder. Some of this is easier to overlook on lower difficulties, but you’ll find the game to be more of a slog than the survival challenge it’s advertised as on harder settings.

A more detailed list of my issues and gripes with the game.
There are essentially two main levels on the game, with a few linear levels sprinkled in between. The third main level is the forest, which is somewhat open world, but has much less to do in it than the other two levels. It feels like they may have had plans to put more content in this one, but ended up cutting it. The rest of the game is some small, linear levels that are meh at best (in my original review I actually completely forgot some of these existed, if that gives any indication of their quality). The game ends with one of these linear levels, which is probably by far the worst level I’ve played in any metro game. I don’t know why the developers thought people would think it was fun to sit in tunnels sniping dozens of tiny plants that will two shot you. If this level had been completely cut from the game it actually would have made it better. Exodus is at it’s best in these two open world levels, especially when the player is able to freely explore and interact with the world.

Boss and wave fights are back and happen in almost every level and you’re locked into these fights, usually as part of the story. Nothing about them is fun, they’re not that short either, and dying to these is also super frustrating since you’ll have to do the entire thing over again. Metro is not an action shooter like COD or something and I have no idea why these things are in a game like Metro and why they’ve been emphasized even more in this title.

Ranger difficulty sucks. I played both of the previous games on ranger, but switched off after a few hours of playing on it. If you ever get into combat on this mode you’ll probably die. Enemies will consistently one shot you with any gun (including shotguns) from hundreds of feet away. This might be okay if you were equally deadly, but enemies will routinely soak up a lot more damage than you could ever take. I’m supposedly to be a highly skilled ranger at this point, so why am I less deadly than some random bandits? Increasing enemy health while decreasing the players is not a good way to do difficulty in shooters. You’re also not allowed to quick save on this mode, so dying can cost you 30+ minutes of progress.

This is tied into a larger issue in that the developers don’t really want you to use guns, or play “loud” in any way. For example, throwing knifes will one shot enemies if they haven’t detected you, but if you’ve been detected throwing knives never one shot enemies and you need to hit them with at least two or three (at least as far as I can tell). How does this make any sense? 
If you want the good ending of the game, you have to stealth and not kill people for most of the game. This means if you’re doing things how you’re ‘supposed to’ a large part of the game will be spent in crouch, slowly stealthing around enemies, hitting E every once in a while to take them down non-lethally. Encouraging stealth isn’t inherently a problem, I had a ton of fun with the Dishonored games, which are built completely around being stealthy. The problem is, Metro is not built around stealth at all. The majority of the stealth gameplay is holding Ctrl, walking at the speed of a snail, and waiting for enemy vision cones to move. 
Even if you’re playing with guns most of them are not that great. The Tihar/crossbow are what you’ll use for the majority of the game because they are silenced and are the only guns it is reasonable to craft ammo for. Their damage is also as good or better than other guns. I never used most of the guns other than switching to them in the middle of a fight instead of reloading because the game gives you no reason to use them. Shotguns are good against some mutants, but there’s actually a surprisingly small number of these encounters so I rarely used it.

Scavenging for resources is basically meaningless and often feels unrewarding. From what I can tell, there are some soft/hard resets of your resources that happen in between levels. So, scavenging for anything more than what you need to get through that level is a waste of time. There’s some story element here about how you’re giving your resources to the crew to help them survive or something, but all this is done behind the scenes, so you never actually know what is going on. If they wanted to limit you on resources or force you to scavenge for your crew I think they should have put some explicit system into the game where you actually give your crew things or can upgrade the Aurora in some way. Just taking away resources from the player for no clear reason feels bad.
Another point on immersion, is that the resource scavenging itself often makes no sense at all. I’ll often loot more ammo from a random toolbox than I get from killing a boss with a minigun. How does this make any sense? There are also places NPC’s will mention that supposedly have big loot hauls, but they never do. In most cases they will have the same amount or loot, or less, than you’d get from any other random place in the game. I think it would have been more fun to make loot concentrated in specific places instead of being spread out absolutely everywhere. I suspect the system was setup this way in order to pad out the game by making the player explore and loot everything.

They’ve also introduced a mechanic into the game where you need to spend resources to clean your guns. Given this, you’d think Artyom would try to keep things clean while exploring, but you’d be wrong. There are so many instances where I’ll just be walking along and Artyom will suddenly decide he needs to take the biggest step in the world and splash himself with all the dirty water he possibly can. Or I’ll be trying to get down from a ledge carefully, but instead Artyom jump down and immerse as much of himself as possible with muck. It makes no sense. It’s pretty obvious this was put into the game as another way to force the player to burn resources.

The developers have also programmed jump scares into the game. It seems like there are a bunch of mutants that are programmed to only react when you physically hit some invisible wall. I’ve run into a couple of these situations where I know enemies are there, but they refuse to move (throwing cans, making noise, or otherwise trying to lure them out does nothing) until I physically get close enough for them to pop out. Kind of weird they can’t hear gunfire right next to them, but my crouched footsteps make enough noise to alert them. There’s a ton of enemies that do this that I didn’t know were there before triggering them, so I’m assuming this kind of thing happens a lot.

I feel Metro Exodus is a step forwards and two step back....

When I first play Metro, it's because it's literally inside a Metro, it was so unique and mind blowing how people built their new life inside a Metro system. There was nothing like this even till today. Only Metro game you get to see it. 

Now having an open world is nice, but I feel the developers were lazy, because the world is fun to explore yet at times feel dead and dull, since there's no real form of missions or any sense of requirement for you to explore. Sure it's better to explore it and get all the best equipment, but you don't actually need it to complete the game. 
It's like you have to use your own imagination to have fun with it....if I were to do that I wouldn't be playing a game, I would learn to be a game developer instead. 

Battles / gunfights are lot more mediocre too....even on the Main Story line, It's not as epic and engaging as the previous two games.
